capability_targets.what_it_does: Create a new CTFd user account (competitor)
List the challenges visible to the current competitor, in bulk
Submit an answer/flag for a challenge and get graded right or wrong
List standings (users or teams) ranked by score
A competitor forms a new team
A competitor joins an existing team by invite code

exemplar.notes: CTFd was verified against the Harvest Admission Rule directly in the cloned repository. LICENSE is the real Apache-2.0 text, matching the spec. Framework: pyproject.toml/requirements.txt pin flask==2.1.3, flask-sqlalchemy==2.5.1, flask-restx==1.3.0 -- Flask confirmed as the production framework. Datastore: this is the one place this pass found the spec's claim needed a caveat rather than an outright correction -- see harvest_source.structural_match and 'unresolved' below for what was actually found about PostgreSQL support. API docs: CTFd/api/__init__.py builds a flask_restx.Api on the '/api/v1' blueprint with 'doc' enabled, which flask_restx serves at '/api/v1/swagger.json' by default -- matches the spec exactly. Structural match verified live: CTFd/api/v1/challenges.py (ChallengeList lists challenges, ChallengeAttempt grades a flag submission correct/incorrect), CTFd/api/v1/scoreboard.py (ScoreboardList ranks standings), CTFd/teams.py (new()/join() are the real self-service create/join-a-team routes) -- the same register/attempt/score/rank shape as TryHackMe, minus TryHackMe's hosted content library.

harvest_source.structural_match: A competitor registers, joins or forms a team, browses challenges worth points, submits an answer which is graded right or wrong, and a leaderboard ranks teams by score over time -- the same register/attempt/score/rank shape as TryHackMe, minus the hosted content library. Verified live: auth.py (register/login/logout), teams.py (new()/join() -- self-service team creation and joining), api/v1/challenges.py (ChallengeList lists challenges, ChallengeAttempt grades a flag submission), api/v1/scoreboard.py (ScoreboardList ranks standings). PostgreSQL caveat: CTFd's config (CTFd/config.ini, docker-compose.yml) defaults to MySQL/MariaDB and its own CHANGELOG states outright 'Postgres is now considered a second class citizen in CTFd. It is tested against but not a main database backend' -- but Postgres is genuinely, not nominally, supported: config.py builds a real SQLAlchemy URL from DATABASE_PROTOCOL (documented, just not defaulted to postgres), the repo carries a dedicated .github/workflows/postgres.yml CI job that runs the real test suite against a real Postgres service container, and CTFd/utils/exports/__init__.py has real Postgres-specific branches (not stub code). Proceeding on that basis; recorded in full in 'unresolved' rather than silently treated as equivalent to Indico/Redash's first-class Postgres support.

capabilities.what_it_does: Creates a new CTFd User from the signup form (name/email/password), applying registration code and visibility settings, then logs the new user in.

side_effects: may send a confirmation email if mail is configured
creates a session for the new user

capabilities.what_it_does: Authenticates a user by name/email + password (or via MajorLeagueCyber OAuth) and starts a session; on success redirects to the page that triggered the login or to /challenges.

side_effects: logs the login in CTFd's login log

capabilities.what_it_does: Clears the current session and redirects to the index page.
Returns every Challenge object visible to the current competitor (respecting visibility, ctf-time-window and email-verification gates), in bulk.
Grades a submitted flag/answer for a challenge (via the challenge type's own attempt() implementation), records a Solves or Fails row, and returns whether it was correct.

dependencies: the challenge type's own attempt() implementation, e.g. CTFd/plugins/dynamic_challenges or the built-in standard type
side_effects: creates a Solves row on a correct submission
creates a Fails row on an incorrect submission

capabilities.what_it_does: Returns the ranked standings (users or teams, depending on the instance's user_mode) ordered by score, for the public scoreboard.
Self-service: a competitor (not yet on a team) creates a new Team, optionally sets a team password, and becomes its captain.

side_effects: adds the current user to it as captain

capabilities.what_it_does: Self-service: a competitor joins an existing team by name and the team's (optional) invite password.

side_effects: adds the current user to the target team's member list

unresolved: datastore / Rule A -- CTFd's own project stance calls Postgres 'a second class citizen... tested against but not a main database backend. If you use Postgres, you are entirely on your own' (CHANGELOG.md), and its default docker-compose/config.ini point at MySQL/MariaDB, not Postgres; psycopg2-binary is listed only in pyproject.toml's dev/test dependency group, not the production requirements.txt. Genuine PostgreSQL support was still confirmed and is not nominal: config.py builds a real SQLAlchemy URL from DATABASE_PROTOCOL (docs just don't default it to postgres), the repo carries its own .github/workflows/postgres.yml CI job running the real pytest suite against a real Postgres service container, and CTFd/utils/exports/__init__.py has real Postgres-specific code branches (not stubs). Proceeding on that basis rather than stopping the app, but recording plainly that 'PostgreSQL' for CTFd means 'supported and CI-tested' rather than 'the primary, defaulted datastore' the way it is for Indico and Redash -- this is a real difference between the three sources, not a copy-paste of the spec's claim.

view_adapter -- left blank, same finding and same reasoning as the Redash form: CTFd's own code never exposes a standalone 'class -> Flask view' bridge function. flask_restx.Api/Namespace registration (CTFd/api/__init__.py, CTFd_API_v1.add_namespace(...)) resolves each Resource class into a view internally inside the flask_restx library, not via any function CTFd itself defines and exports. No adapter symbol was found to name, so it is left blank per the spec's instruction rather than invented.

register / log in / log out / create team / join team -- all five are genuinely plain Flask blueprint functions in CTFd's own source (auth.py, teams.py), confirmed by grep across the whole repository for MethodView/.as_view( usage outside CTFd/api/ -- there is none. Every class-based view in CTFd is a flask_restx.Resource under /api/v1/*. This was not a choice among alternatives: CTFd genuinely has no class-based implementation of register/login/logout/create-team/join-team to harvest instead. Combined with the blank view_adapter above, host.py's bind_shelf_parts (which only binds a symbol that resolves to a class -- 'isinstance(obj, type)') is expected to refuse all five of these with 'part has no class named by ...'; the three class-based capabilities (list challenges, submit flag, view scoreboard) are expected to resolve to a class but, with no adapter, be bound as the raw class rather than a proper view function -- what actually happens at request time is exactly what the host run records, not assumed here.

models_loader -- left blank. CTFd:create_app itself does 'from CTFd.models import (... db)' and calls db.create_all()/upgrade() and every app.register_blueprint(...) inline before returning the built app, so there is no separate lazy model-registration step to name.

data_filename / data_shape.data_access -- left blank on every capability, same reasoning as the other two apps: CTFd's real persistence is PostgreSQL/MySQL via SQLAlchemy models (Users, Teams, Challenges, Solves, Fails -- real tables), not a flat JSON file per entity.

shared_lib_calls -- left empty on every capability. CTFd implements its own session (Flask session cookie + itsdangerous), password hashing (passlib, via Users.password) and its own scoring/ranking logic -- none of it calls CAP-0000's shared library.

run.start_command / run.port -- CTFd's own documented entry point (serve.py / 'flask run', default port 8000 in this repo's docker-compose.yml); not run live this session outside of host.py, recorded for completeness of the form's 'run' block.
